title: The funnel looks healthy — right up until the last step.
body: Every stakeholder had a theory — price, competition, shipping. Nobody had looked at the screen the user was actually looking at. The brief said "make it convert", and that is a trap when you don't know which step is bleeding.
quote: Feels fine until I have to commit.

notes.text: The funnel looks healthy until "Proceed to checkout".
No security signals — the page asks for money before it says one reassuring word.
The price is everywhere. Trust is nowhere.

title: Five of six recordings froze on the very same field.
body: No participant found the page suspicious — they simply refused to commit. I interviewed twelve people who had dropped off in the last thirty days and ran a heuristic walkthrough of the flow.
quote: Nothing's wrong with this page. I just don't want to give it my card.

notes.text: 65% of drop-offs happen here — not in cart, not in shipping.
Fees only appear after the card number.
No PCI or "secured by" cue anywhere.

title: On the most common phone size, the Pay button does not exist.
body: The keyboard swallows the primary action. Users who made it to payment had to scroll, guess, and pray the button would surface.
quote: Where did the pay button go?

notes.text: The keyboard pushes the CTA off-screen.
The most common device class — that is, your actual users.

title: The gateway is a contractual red line. The trap it creates is not.
body: I could not change the pricing model or the payment provider. I could move every cost the user would ever see to the top of the screen, and stop building a trap where the final price appears only after commitment. Fix the experience, report the policy problem, and never design around it.

title: A checkout that says "everything is clear" before it asks for money.
body: Fees declared up front. Trust markers placed exactly where the eye lands. A payment step that survives the mobile keyboard. Then I measured — because a good design is a hypothesis that has not been tested yet.

notes.text: Fees declared up front — no surprise step later.
Trust markers exactly where the eye lands.
The Pay button survives the keyboard.

title: 60% → 35%. The company stopped blaming the price.
body: The drop-off curve flattened after three A/B tests and one shipped variant. The fix took six weeks. The theory took six days to dismantle.
quote: It wasn't the price. Nobody had looked at the screen.

notes.text: The change survived two A/B tests and a post-launch audit.

title: The flow is fixed. The pricing policy is still hiding.
body: I would run the A/B test three weeks earlier — and treat "surprise fee discovery" as a product decision, not just a UX one. Users do not abandon a checkout because they are uninterested. They abandon because something in the system told them, quietly, not to trust.
